title: meta-analysis.cz: harmonised estimate-level data from meta-analyses in economics
description:
Estimate-level data from meta-analyses in economics and the social sciences, with the study and design characteristics hand-coded for each original paper.

What this deposit contains. The harmonised estimate-level table pooling 42 economics meta-analysis literatures, the machine-readable dataset index, a column-level codebook for each of the 46 source datasets, and the documentation. It does NOT contain the per-dataset format conversions, the papers themselves, or their replication packages; those remain at https://meta-analysis.cz.

What the numbers mean. 46 datasets contain 67,606 rows in the converted source files. After each paper's own filters, applied where its replication code defines them as a row filter on the stored scale and otherwise keeping the rows that carry a usable standard error, and where necessary a reshape of wide data into estimate-level form, those become 56,046 harmonisable estimates. Two consequences worth stating: frisch's paper retains rows whose standard error it imputes by bootstrap, which cannot be reproduced from the published files, so those rows are dropped here; and skill's selection requires transforming the effect, so it is not applied. The harmonised table pools 50,441 of them across 42 literatures. Each dataset also ships a column-level codebook.

Changes since 1.2.1. frisch now carries both margins the paper reports, in one dataset. The intertemporal substitution elasticity of labour supply is estimated on an intensive margin (hours, given that you work) and an extensive margin (whether you work), and the paper reports over 700 estimates on each. Until now only the extensive margin was published as a dataset: 762 estimates from 38 studies. The intensive margin, 709 estimates from 40 studies, shipped inside frisch/frisch_data.zip but was invisible to anything reading the API and absent from the pooled table. It is now included, with a margin column distinguishing the two, the same way a dataset carrying short-run and long-run estimates flags them rather than dropping one.

The dataset therefore goes from 762 rows to 1,471, and contributes 1,128 rows to the pooled table instead of 553. The study count is 57, not 78: 21 papers report on both margins, and study ids are keyed on the study label so such a paper keeps one id across the pair. Each file keeps its own idcoeff, the paper's within-study estimate number, untouched, so within this dataset the unique key is (margin, idstudy, idcoeff); the pooled table's estimate_id is assigned per dataset by the pipeline and is unique there. The two files name two moderators differently, no_obs against obs and pub_year against pubyear; these are coalesced, so neither margin loses a moderator it actually recorded.

The two margins are different outcomes and must not be averaged together. They are shipped together because they are one literature and the paper reports both. Filter before pooling: margin in the per-dataset file, and source_file in the harmonised table, which names the member each row came from (data_extensive.xlsx or data_intensive.xlsx) because margin itself does not survive harmonisation.

This is a general limitation of the harmonised table, not something specific to frisch, and it is worth stating plainly. The table carries no column for a sub-outcome within a literature. gasoline_price pools 110 short-run and 92 long-run elasticities with nothing at all to tell them apart, because its source's longr dummy does not survive harmonisation either; electricity and gasoline are the same case. Where a sub-outcome matters to your question, go to the per-dataset file, which keeps every moderator the source recorded. frisch is currently the only literature whose sub-outcomes can be separated from the pooled table alone.

Nothing else moved. Row counts for the other 41 literatures are unchanged, the harmonised table's columns are unchanged, and every row published in 1.2.1 carries the same effect, standard error and t-statistic here; the 553 extensive rows also keep their 1.2.1 study_id and estimate_id, so anyone who used only that margin is unaffected. The per-dataset file necessarily gains columns: margin, source_member and source_study_id (the workbook's own study number, kept because the shared key is re-keyed), plus the moderators each margin records and the other does not. Two source quirks are worth knowing: five columns are populated for extensive rows only and four for intensive rows only, and Attanasio et al. is dated 2018 in one file and 2017 in the other, so that one study carries two publication years in the per-dataset file. It does not reach the pooled table, because none of those rows has a usable standard error.

Metadata corrections in this release. Five records said something inaccurate, none of which changed a published number. frisch's reconciliation reported the paper's count as 700, which is what an automatic read of "over 700 estimates" returns although the paper says that of each margin separately, and its arithmetic was against a stale row count; it now states the counts explicitly. bma and spillovers still declared their units as "elasticity" in the pipeline's own override file, although the published records were corrected to semi-elasticity in 1.2.1; the input now agrees with the output. CITATION.cff labelled DOI 22050272 as version 1.2.0, which is wrong, that is 1.1.1, and it had dropped 22212666 (the real 1.2.0) from the record entirely; the version history is rewritten and every version now maps to the identifier it was published under.

A clarification about skill, which reusers should read. The pooled table takes the 965 rows of that dataset's 1,097 that carry a usable standard error, on the stored substitution-elasticity scale. That is not the paper's own analysis sample: the paper analyses the rows it flags as inverted, 683 from 77 studies in the file against the 682 the paper reports, after computing the negative reciprocal of the stored column, as this dataset's direction_note sets out; only 654 of those carry a standard error, so the paper's exact headline sample is not reproducible from the published file alone. Both quantities are recoverable from what is published, but anyone reproducing the paper's headline must apply that transformation and that subset rather than taking these rows as they stand. More generally, "each paper's own analysis selection" is applied where the paper's replication code defines one; where that selection is a row filter on the stored scale. Where reproducing it would require transforming the effect, as in skill, it is not applied, and the selection is the rows carrying a usable standard error.

Rows are not always independent estimates. The harmonised table holds one row per harmonised observation. Two literatures are impulse responses: price_puzzle contributes 1,395 rows across seven horizons, and house_prices contributes 1,555 rows at one row per impulse-response horizon, so rows within a single response function are not independent of each other. Use the horizon column before treating rows as independent observations. frisch now needs the same care for a different reason: split on source_file, which distinguishes the two margins.

Review status: every literature has been checked against its source. All 42 pooled literatures are verified, with the evidence quoted per dataset: 22 reviewed against the paper's own replication code or published results by hand, and 20 confirmed mechanically by reading each paper's code and comparing the variables it regresses with the columns published here. gasoline_price ships no replication code at all and was therefore verified against its paper's published results directly: the abstract reports a corrected long-run elasticity of -0.31 and short-run of -0.09, with published averages "exaggerated twofold", and the shipped data gives means of -0.691 and -0.227, reproducing that twofold exaggeration and the long-run/short-run ordering. Every dataset publishes an audit_status.

Known defects in this release. 75 class estimates are inconsistent with the source column's own partial-correlation construction: 2 lie outside [-1, 1] and 73 sit at exactly plus or minus 1 while carrying a positive standard error. They are concentrated in one study, and publication-bias inference for that literature is not robust to them: an unweighted regression of effect on standard error changes sharply when they are excluded, while a precision-weighted FAT-PET on the same data does not. A further 82 class rows store a partial correlation of exactly zero beside a non-zero t-statistic; those are excluded from the pooled table by that literature's own analysis selection. Separately, 1,510 rows across 39 literatures are identical to another row in every column except estimate_id. Those are not manufactured, the source files carry them, so running drop_duplicates() as routine hygiene will delete real estimates: deduplicate on (dataset, estimate_id), which is unique by construction.

Changes since 1.2.0. 1.2.1 corrected three datasets that were being read or labelled wrongly. frisch was reading a loose 723-row draft file matching neither sample its paper reports, and was pinned to the published extensive-margin file. activism was shipping a second header row as an estimate, 1,974 against the paper's 1,973. lags named the VAR lag order as its outcome where the same record's direction note described the months to the price trough. It also relabelled spillovers and bma as semi-elasticities, corrected skill's direction note (keeping the wrong text in direction_note_correction, because a reader who acted on it needs to know), and published the publication year that finance_growth and inflation always held.

Changes since 1.1.1. 1.2.0 corrected n_obs on 4,614 rows: armington and migrant were publishing the number of ESTIMATES a study reports as its sample size, which is not the same quantity and silently corrupts any estimator that uses the sample size, the first stage of MAIVE among them. armington now carries each study's real sample size, and migrant carries none, because no sample size can be recovered from its source. If you ran either literature out of the 1.1.1 archive with a method that uses n, rerun it against this version. 1.2.0 also added cbequity: 176 partial correlations from 9 studies on central bank equity and monetary policy, the 46th dataset and the 42nd pooled literature.

Changes since 1.0.0. 1.1.0 added finance_growth as a 45th dataset. 1.1.1 removes 20 price_puzzle rows that corresponded to no source estimate: the reshape deduplicated on every column except the horizon rather than on the source's own impulse-response identifier, and three blocks each carried one inconsistent month-code cell, so each split in two. The source declares 217 impulse responses where the pipeline had built 220. No published statistic moves: the counts either side of an absolute t-statistic of 1.96 are 508 and 633 before and after, and every removed row had an absolute t below 1.57. 1.1.0 was served live for about a day and was never deposited.

Changes since 0.9.0-beta. 1.0.0 corrected defects found by an independent audit of the beta files. price_puzzle repeated every estimate seven times, because its source file is already long on the impulse-response horizon while its response columns are wide and the reshape did not deduplicate; it now carries 1,395 rows across all seven horizons, including the trough and peak responses that the beta discarded entirely. remittances published the raw regression coefficients its source file carries, over five different dependent variables; it now publishes the partial correlations its paper actually analyses. pub_year held a standardised model regressor rather than a publication year in five literatures, because the column was matched by name; year columns are now validated by value. trust is newly included, contributing the 284 estimates that size does not already carry. t_stat and precision are now derived in double precision throughout.

Read the weight concentration before benchmarking. Each dataset publishes max_precision_weight_share, the share of total inverse-variance weight held by its single most precise estimate. In several literatures one estimate carries more than half, and in three it carries essentially all of it, because the original paper rounded a standard error to a very small value. Any precision-weighted estimator on those literatures returns approximately that one observation, so a comparison of estimators there measures very little. Check this field before drawing conclusions.

Which column holds the effect and which its standard error was resolved arithmetically rather than by name: the correct pair is the one for which the effect divided by its standard error reproduces the t-statistic the dataset already reports. Where that was not decisive, the mapping was taken from the paper's own published replication code, or from identifying what the rival column actually is, and that evidence is recorded per dataset.

Every row of the harmonised table carries the source file and the exact column names it came from, so any value can be traced back to the published dataset and checked. Effects are not comparable across literatures in raw units; an effect_units column records what each one measures, and a direction note records the sign conventions that would otherwise trap a reanalyst.
